newsitem.title: UK: Sterling rides high as market's budget fears ease.
newsitem.headline: Sterling rides high as market's budget fears ease.

text.p: Sterling hit the high spots again in Europe on Tuesday, fuelled by optimism about the British economy and confidence that the government can actually afford the tax cuts it is so keen to make in next week's budget.

The latest fillip for a pound locked in steep bull trends against its major currency partners came from data showing the government repaid a hefty 4.4 billion sterling of public debt in October, boosted by a flood of corporate tax receipts.
Subsequent talk of rate rises helped sterling to four-year peaks versus the dollar and near 30-month highs on the mark.
Analysts were confident Chancellor Kenneth Clarke would use his elbow-room to cut taxes modestly at the November 26 budget, reduce spending and bring down public sector borrowing.

"Clearly the figures flatter the government's position and give room for more tinkering around than otherwise thought -- but I suspect wiser counsels will prevail," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London.
The Conservative government, trailing in opinion polls and facing a general election which must be held by next May, has made no secret of its desire to make vote-wooing tax cuts.
But persistent market fears that the Conservatives could sacrifice economic prudence for votes have been largely soothed by Monday's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) data.

"One of the few remaining negatives for sterling has perhaps been removed. People are more relaxed, they think (Clarke) is going to keep things relatively tight and he'll be able to afford it," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"If he can combine that with a downward revision to next year's PSBR forecast, then he has his cake and eats it."
Fear of a fiscally-imprudent budget was indeed one of the few remaining thorns in sterling's side.
With the market hungry for yield, a rash of economic data pointing to a healthy British economy has fired up speculation of monetary tightening and thereby benefited the pound.
The sharp rally against the mark began in early August, when the Bank of England said a rate rise would be needed to restrain inflation. The increase eventually came through on October 30.
The pound has risen nearly 11 percent versus the mark since August 5 and more than 12 percent on the dollar since May 1, touching new highs of 2.5193 marks and $1.6765 on Tuesday.
Higher than expected retail prices released last week boosted the pound as talk of further tightening hotted up.
One simple factor in sterling's bull run is the fact that it has lagged units such as the lira and peseta, analysts said.

"Sterling was the only currency in 1996 not to recover from its record lows in 1995," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch. "Given that the UK had among the highest yields in Europe, that situation was unsustainable.

"People did generally perceive value in sterling but the political risk premium distorted the picture and left the market very underweight in sterling when the currency was quite clearly undervalued within a European context," Prendergast said.

Although the market appears happier now that the Chancellor will deliver a sensible budget -- a one-penny cut in the basic rate of income tax is thought to be priced in -- analysts said even bigger tax giveaways might not hurt the pound unduly.

Standard Chartered's Fox said a cut of more than a penny would stir up already widespread talk of another rate rise after the December monetary meeting between Clarke and the Bank of England governor Eddie George.

"Sterling would probably take it positively in the current climate," said Fox. "You'd see it coming off with gilts and equities but then you might feel the interest rate argument would prevail and bring it back up again."
